title: Nala and Damayanti
hook: Damayanti wakes alone in half a cloth, and walks through the forest asking mountains and trees for her husband

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nala and Damayanti shared one cloth in the forest, until he cut it in the dark and left. Who did you notice staying beside you? Day seven hundred ninety-two.

Half a cloth. That's what Damayanti finds when she wakes on the floor of the empty rest house. Half of the garment they shared, and no husband. She calls his name. She runs through the trees calling it, half thinking he's hiding, playing some cruel game. Come out, she says, I'm frightened. Nobody answers. Only the trees, and the empty road, and her own voice coming back. And the story, which has followed Nala until now, turns and follows her.
screen: `HALF A CLOTH.` → `SHE CALLS HIS NAME.` → `THE STORY FOLLOWS HER.`

segments.voice: Her first thought, the story says, is for him: who will look after him now, hungry and alone in the forest? Then the forest closes in. A huge serpent seizes her, and even in its coils she cries out for Nala, not for herself. A hunter hears her, kills the snake and frees her. Then he looks at her the wrong way. She sees what he intends. And Damayanti, who has nothing, no husband, no clothes, no kingdom, still has the force of her own faithfulness. In the story it's enough. She curses him, and the hunter falls dead. Then she walks. And as she walks, she talks to everything. She asks a mountain whether it has seen a king named Nala. She meets a group of ascetics who tell her she'll see Nala again, and then they vanish, hermitage and all. She comes to an Ashoka tree in bloom, and the tree's name means without sorrow, and she asks it to live up to its name: take my sorrow, tell me where he went. The tree doesn't answer. She joins a band of traveling merchants. In the night, wild elephants crash through their camp, and in the morning some of the survivors look at the strange half-dressed woman and wonder aloud whether she brought them bad luck. At last she comes to the city of Chedi, ragged, and the queen mother sees her from a window and takes her in. Damayanti agrees to serve, on her own terms: she will keep her dignity, and she won't speak with men who come seeking her. Look at her. She lost the same things Nala lost, and then she lost Nala too. But she never stops asking where he is.
screen: `THE SERPENT AND THE HUNTER.` · `SHE ASKS A MOUNTAIN.` · `"ASHOKA, TAKE MY SORROW."` · then, large: `SHE NEVER STOPS ASKING.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath slow. Damayanti spoke to the mountains and the trees because there was no one else to tell. Choose one thing near you that's been there through a hard season: a window, a plant, a mug, a street outside. Rest your eyes on it, or picture it. Breathe in. Breathe out. Let it be a quiet witness for a moment, without asking anything of it. If you pray, you can bring whatever you've been carrying into your prayer. If not, simply let the thing in front of you keep you company. The bell holds the time.
Nala and Damayanti. Today, Damayanti alone: a serpent, a hunter, an Ashoka tree, a caravan, a city, and one question asked of everything she meets.
Your line: Nala and Damayanti. Today, keep asking the one question that matters to you, even if nothing answers yet. Day seven hundred ninety-two.

howItsDone: Damayanti's wandering, from the forest to the court of Chedi, is told in the Nala story of the Mahabharata's Vana Parva, where her lament to the Ashoka tree plays on the tree's name, 'without sorrow'.

beg him to let you go.

original.note: Sanskrit ashoka: without sorrow, the name of the flowering tree Damayanti asks to take her grief.

trapdoor: what you thought: once Nala left, the story would follow him.
what it means: it turns and follows Damayanti, who keeps searching through every danger.
what a scholar hears: Damayanti's lament plays on the Ashoka tree's name, a-shoka, without sorrow.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Nalopakhyana: Damayanti wakes; the serpent and the hunter; her lament to the mountain and the Ashoka tree; the ascetics; the merchants and the elephants; the court of Chedi)

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm that Damayanti's lament to the Ashoka tree plays on its name (a-shoka, 'without sorrow'), as the trapdoor and original state; this is the text's own wordplay, not a preacher's etymology, but verify in Ganguli.
Confirm the order: serpent, hunter, mountain, ascetics, Ashoka tree, merchants, elephants, Chedi. The teach may have the mountain/tree/ascetics order slightly off.

Damayanti's conditions for service at Chedi are summarized loosely ('keep her dignity', 'won't speak with men who come seeking her'); confirm the list (not eating leavings, not washing feet, not speaking with other men).
The hunter's death by Damayanti's curse is in the text; the framing 'the force of her own faithfulness' paraphrases her appeal to her chastity.
